questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define incrementalism as a theory of policy change
questions.stem: Revision note REV-101 asks the group to define incrementalism as a theory of how public policy changes.

options.text: Change proceeds by small, regular adjustments to existing policy rather than by wholesale redesign.
Change proceeds quickly whenever a government is willing to act without consultation.
options.misconception: confuses incrementalism with decisive, rapid reform

options.text: Change happens only when a crisis makes the existing policy impossible to sustain.
options.misconception: restricts change to moments of crisis

options.text: Change is produced by the gradual improvement of the skill of each new policy team.
options.misconception: reads incrementalism as a claim about personnel quality

questions.explanation: Incrementalism treats policy as adjustment to what already exists, in small regular steps. The distractors substitute speed, crisis and staff quality for that account of how change occurs.
questions.hint: Ask how large each step of change is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the pattern of change punctuated equilibrium predicts
questions.stem: Revision note REV-104 asks the group to describe the pattern of change that punctuated equilibrium predicts.

options.text: Policy changes steadily, with each adjustment a little larger than the last one.
options.misconception: confuses stasis and bursts with steady growth

options.text: Policy changes rapidly for a period and then settles into stability for a long time.
options.misconception: reverses the order of stasis and bursts

options.text: Policy stays stable for long periods and then changes sharply in a short burst.
Policy changes only in response to the annual cycle of the budget and the electoral calendar.
options.misconception: attributes change only to the institutional calendar

questions.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium predicts long periods of near-stability broken by short, sharp bursts of change. The distractors describe steady growth and confine change to the timetable.
questions.hint: Ask what happens just before a burst.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many review cycles a policy horizon contains
questions.stem: Revision note REV-107 asks the group to work out how many three-yearly review cycles fit into a policy horizon of 27 years.
questions.explanation: Twenty-seven years divided by three-year cycles gives nine reviews. The tempting error counts the starting year as an extra cycle, producing ten.
questions.hint: Divide the years by the cycle length.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a policy feedback effect in a loan scheme
questions.stem: Revision note REV-112 asks the group to identify an example of policy feedback inside a student loan scheme.

options.text: The scheme raises the repayment threshold, so graduates repay over more years.
options.misconception: treats a design change as a feedback effect

options.text: The scheme is administered by a department that issues guidance to universities.
options.misconception: confuses administrative guidance with feedback

options.text: The scheme replaces an earlier loan scheme that had different repayment terms.
options.misconception: treats policy replacement as a feedback effect

options.text: Graduates on higher incomes repay more, which funds further support for lower-income students.

questions.explanation: Feedback occurs when a policy changes the resources or preferences of the actors it affects, which then shapes later politics. The distractors describe design, administration and replacement.
questions.hint: Ask who changes their behaviour because of the policy.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Characterise coverage that displaces a technical question

stimulus.body: A national daily ran a headline about children losing access to a woodland school, supported by a photograph of a child at a gate, and the item was shared widely before the council debated the proposal. The proposal itself concerned a change to how the woodland schools were inspected, and the inspection method was not mentioned in the coverage at all.

questions.stem: Revision note REV-115 asks the group to characterise the coverage described in the extract.

options.text: The coverage is a straightforward report of the inspection change the council debated.
options.misconception: misses the mismatch between framing and content

options.text: The coverage is a technical report, because the item explained the inspection method.
options.misconception: assumes technical detail the extract lacks

options.text: The coverage is a morality play because the policy itself was morally indefensible.
options.misconception: confuses moral framing with moral failure

options.text: The coverage is a morality play, because a moral image displaced the technical question.

questions.explanation: A morality play carries a moral framing that pushes a technical issue out of view. The distractors misread the content, invent detail the extract lacks, and confuse framing with moral failure.
questions.hint: Ask which question the coverage pushed aside.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret figures that show a delivery shortfall
questions.stem: Revision note REV-119 gives the group's figures: a flood defence scheme was approved at a budget of 2.4 million, and 1.9 million of it was spent delivering 11 of the 14 planned barriers, and asks the group to interpret them.

options.text: Delivery fell short of the plan, so the gap between decision and outcome is visible here.
Delivery is a success, because most of the approved budget was spent on the scheme.
options.misconception: treats budget use as evidence of delivered outcomes

options.text: The figures prove the scheme failed, because 11 barriers is too few to matter.
options.misconception: judges the scheme by an invented threshold

options.text: The figures show the budget was badly set, because the cost per barrier stayed the same.
options.misconception: invents a cost comparison the figures do not give

questions.explanation: A gap between what was decided and what was delivered is the implementation gap in the numbers. The distractors read budget use as success and invent a threshold or cost comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what was planned against what happened.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how standard operating procedures produce predictability
questions.stem: Revision note REV-124 asks the group to explain how standard operating procedures make a bureaucratic organisation predictable.

options.text: They give officers discretion to handle each case as the circumstances require.
options.misconception: confuses routine rules with case-by-case discretion

options.text: They place every decision with the senior officer in charge of the unit.
options.misconception: confuses standardisation with hierarchy

options.text: They fix the steps for routine cases, so similar cases are handled the same way.
They remove the need for training, because the rules speak for themselves.
options.misconception: assumes standardisation removes the need for expertise

questions.explanation: Standard operating procedures achieve predictability by fixing how routine cases are handled. The distractors substitute case-by-case discretion, hierarchy and the removal of training.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a routine case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the source of red tape in a licensing office
questions.stem: Revision note REV-128 asks the group to identify the source of red tape in a licensing office.

options.text: The office employs too many staff, so no single person is accountable for the outcome.
options.misconception: attributes red tape to staffing levels

options.text: The office requires several separate approvals that no single official can grant.
The office sets a high standard that most applicants cannot meet at first attempt.
options.misconception: confuses a substantive standard with procedural burden

options.text: The office publishes its targets, and staff feel pressure to meet them quickly.
options.misconception: treats published targets as a cause of delay

questions.explanation: Red tape is the procedural burden that separate rules and approvals impose on a case. The distractors blame staffing, confuse a standard with procedure, and blame published targets.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish merit recruitment from patronage appointment
questions.stem: Revision note REV-132 asks the group to explain what distinguishes merit recruitment from patronage appointment.

answer.exemplar: Merit recruitment appoints people on the basis of assessed ability against published criteria, while patronage appointment uses public office to reward political support. The difference is not only in the slogan but in the procedure that accompanies it: a competitive process with a written test, a scored shortlist and a recorded decision generates a record that can be examined later, whereas an appointment made to reward a supporter leaves nothing to check and can be presented as discretion. Merit recruitment also protects the incoming administration, because officials appointed on the previous administration's criteria are less likely to be judged as politically partisan, and it makes turnover less disruptive. The defensible answer is therefore about procedure and auditability as much as about fairness in the abstract.

questions.explanation: Merit recruitment rests on published criteria and a recordable process, while patronage rewards support. The tempting contrast, that one is fair and the other is not, misses the procedural difference.
questions.hint: Ask what record the process leaves behind.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a growing queue from administrative data
questions.stem: Revision note REV-136 gives figures: a licensing queue moved from 80 to 110 applications over a year while the team size and the rules both stayed the same, and asks the group to interpret the change.

options.text: The queue grew because the rules were quietly changed to make approval harder.
options.misconception: assumes a rule change the figures rule out

options.text: The queue grew because the team became less efficient under new management.
options.misconception: blames staff effort without evidence

options.text: The queue grew because more residents applied for licences than in the previous year.
options.misconception: explains the queue without checking the arrival rate

options.text: The queue grew, so demand rose faster than the unchanged capacity could absorb.

questions.explanation: With rules and staffing fixed, a growing queue points to more arrivals than the office can process. The distractors invent a rule change, blame effort, and assert demand without evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed the same while the queue grew.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that incrementalism makes change easy to reverse
questions.stem: Revision note REV-140 asks the group to evaluate the claim that incrementalism makes policy change easy to reverse.

options.text: It is defensible, because small steps leave the existing programme in place to fall back on.
It is defensible, because incremental changes attract less public attention than large ones.
options.misconception: grounds reversibility in low attention

options.text: It is indefensible, because incrementalism prevents any policy from being changed at all.
options.misconception: confuses incrementalism with an absence of change

options.text: It is indefensible, because reversibility would reward the officials who made the mistake.
options.misconception: assumes reversal always benefits the wrong people

questions.explanation: Small, additive adjustments can be undone one at a time because the previous arrangement survives underneath them. The distractors shift the ground to attention and assume reversal punishes officials.
questions.hint: Ask what remains in place if a step is reversed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a punctuating burst in a policy timeline

stimulus.body: The note records that a ministerial programme of small annual adjustments to benefit rates ran for 11 years without major change. In the twelfth year, following a legal challenge and a new minister, the whole schedule was replaced in a single decision, and the note records that three separate long-standing rates were abolished rather than adjusted.

questions.stem: Revision note REV-144 asks the group to identify the feature of the timeline that fits punctuated equilibrium.

options.text: The eleven years of small adjustments, since each was a discrete change to a published rate.
options.misconception: reads routine adjustment as a burst of change

options.text: The replacement in year twelve, because a single decision can always be described as a change.
options.misconception: treats any single decision as a punctuating burst

options.text: The abolition of three rates at once, after eleven years of no comparable change.
The change of minister, because personnel changes are the usual cause of policy change.
options.misconception: explains bursts by a change of personnel

questions.explanation: A punctuating burst is a substantial change after long stasis, and abolishing three rates together fits that pattern. The distractors read routine adjustment as a burst and blame personnel.
questions.hint: Ask what the contrast is between.

questions.explanation: Two reductions of 15 per cent leave 70 per cent of the original policy, provided the second applies to what remained. The tempting error treats the second change as a share of the original.
questions.hint: Apply each change to what is left.

questions.learningObjective: Challenge the claim that a fee change has no feedback effects
questions.stem: Revision note REV-152 asks the group to assess the claim that a tuition fee policy has no feedback effects because it only changes the price charged.

options.text: The claim is right, because the price is set by statute and cannot be adapted.
options.misconception: assumes statutory prices rule out adaptive responses

options.text: The claim is right, because the number of students is set by the funding formula.
options.misconception: treats a formula as fixing student numbers

options.misconception: assumes institutions cannot adapt their behaviour

options.text: The claim is doubtful, because higher fees change who studies and how institutions respond.

questions.explanation: Prices change behaviour, and those changes feed back into later politics and funding. The distractors assume a statutory price, a formula and institutional rigidity all prevent adjustment.
questions.hint: Ask what the price changes besides the invoice.

questions.learningObjective: Contrast moral and technical campaign framings
questions.stem: Revision note REV-156 compares two campaigns: one argued that a new national standard for building safety would raise construction costs, and the other argued that families were being let down by unsafe homes, and asks the group to contrast them.

options.text: The first is a morality play, because it appeals to the concerns of builders.
options.misconception: treats any interest appeal as a morality play

options.text: The second is a technical argument, because unsafe homes are a measurable standard.
options.misconception: assumes measurable claims are never moral

options.text: Both are morality plays, because neither mentions a specific cost figure.
options.misconception: infers morality play from a missing figure

options.text: The second is a morality play, because a moral appeal displaced the technical question.

questions.explanation: A morality play displaces a technical issue with a moral frame that mobilises support. The distractors treat any interest appeal as moral and infer it from a missing number.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an implementation gap appears
questions.stem: Revision note REV-160 asks the group to explain why an implementation gap appears between an approved policy and what citizens experience.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the main source of delay in a case

stimulus.body: A small food business reported that its licence application was returned three times, each time for a different document, and that it took eleven weeks to complete. An officer noted that the business had been asked for its floor plan twice and for its food hygiene rating twice, and that the checklist available to officers had been revised three times in the previous two years.

questions.stem: Revision note REV-168 asks the group to identify the main source of delay described in the case.

options.text: The delay comes mainly from the business failing to keep proper records of its own details.
options.misconception: blames the applicant for the repeated requests

options.text: The delay comes from a patchwork of overlapping requirements and an unstable checklist.
The delay comes mainly from officers taking longer to read each document than necessary.
options.misconception: blames individual reading speed

options.text: The delay comes mainly from the fee charged for the licence, which discourages early applications.
options.misconception: invents a fee motive the case does not mention

questions.explanation: Repeated requests for the same item and a thrice-revised checklist point to an unstable, overlapping rule set. The distractors blame records, reading speed and a fee.
questions.hint: Ask what the checklist did over two years.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the argument that more caseworkers shorten queues
questions.stem: Revision note REV-176 asks the group to evaluate the argument that adding more caseworkers to a benefits office will reduce waiting times.

answer.exemplar: The argument identifies the right target but the wrong lever, and the team should be able to say why. A backlog is usually not caused by a shortage of people alone; it is produced by a process in which cases are routed through several separate checks, each with its own queue, and by the simple arithmetic of arrival rate against throughput. Adding staff to a badly designed process produces more staff moving cases through the same number of steps, which may shorten the queue at one point and lengthen the total time elsewhere. The defensible conclusion is that staffing matters most once the process has been simplified and the points of duplication removed, and that a staffing increase on its own should be expected to give a smaller improvement than the argument assumes.

questions.explanation: Backlogs usually come from the design of the process, so more staff on the same steps gives less improvement than expected. The tempting view that delay is purely staffing ignores duplication.
questions.hint: Ask what the added staff would work on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge the claim that incrementalism is only a description of behaviour
questions.stem: Revision note REV-180 asks the group to judge the claim that incrementalism is simply a realistic description of how politicians behave.

options.text: The claim is justified, because politicians are conservative creatures in practice.
options.misconception: accepts a behavioural claim as an analytical one

options.text: The claim is justified, because large reforms are never attempted in practice.
options.misconception: reads realism as evidence of impossibility

options.text: The claim is justified, because no party has ever proposed a wholesale reform.
options.misconception: makes a historical claim the note does not support

options.text: The claim is doubtful, because incrementalism is a claim about bias in the whole system.

questions.explanation: Incrementalism argues that the system's structure biases choice towards small steps, rather than describing cautious politicians. The distractors treat it as a claim about behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about people or structure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what punctuating events are in the account
questions.stem: Revision note REV-184 asks the group to state what punctuating events are in the punctuated equilibrium account of policymaking.

answer.exemplar: Punctuating events are the moments in which a period of stability is broken by a change large enough to reset the agenda, and they usually arrive as a problem framed so that it cannot be handled by adjustment. In the account the group is revising, a decision is normally reached by bargaining among participants who each want a modest, affordable adjustment, so the system settles into a stable configuration and stays there. What punctuates it is a shock that raises the cost of leaving that configuration: a scandal, a crisis, a change in the composition of the decision-makers, or a reframing that makes the status quo morally indefensible. The important point for the revision is that the events are not only crises, and that their size and their unpredictability are what distinguish them from ordinary revision of an existing policy.

questions.explanation: Punctuating events are shocks that make the status quo untenable and reset the agenda. The tempting account, that they are only crises, ignores reframing and changes in the participants as well.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the status quo untenable.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret contrasting evidence about policy durability
questions.stem: Revision note REV-188 gives figures: a policy introduced in 2004 survived two changes of government and was still being applied in 2024, while a policy introduced in 2014 was withdrawn after its sponsor left office, and asks the group to interpret the contrast.

options.text: The 2004 policy survived because it was better designed than the 2014 policy.
options.misconception: assumes design quality explains durability

options.text: The 2014 policy was withdrawn because it was too new to be defended.
options.misconception: treats age as the sole defence of a policy

options.text: Durability depends on support that outlasts the officeholders who created it.
The 2004 policy survived because it had more resources attached to it.
options.misconception: assumes funding explains durability

questions.explanation: A policy that outlasts two changes of government has built support beyond its sponsors, which is what durability means. The distractors attribute survival to design and withdrawal to youth.
questions.hint: Ask what the policy outlived.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the feedback effect of an energy saving payment

options.text: Households install insulation, which then makes further efficiency cheaper to achieve.

questions.learningObjective: Assess a campaign through the morality play account

options.text: The campaign failed, because the technical assessment was the more important issue.

options.misconception: assumes publicity substitutes for inquiry

questions.explanation: A morality play is a moral framing that pushes a narrow technical question out of view and mobilises action. The distractors treat a moral campaign as technical and substitute publicity for inquiry.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret data comparing approval steps and waiting times
questions.stem: Revision note REV-208 gives figures: a grant scheme processed 240 applications with 9 separate approval steps each, taking a median of 74 days, and a revised scheme with 4 steps took a median of 46 days, and asks the group to interpret them.

options.text: The revised scheme was slower, because 46 days is longer than the 28-day reduction in the figures.
options.misconception: misreads a change in the median as the new waiting time

options.text: Fewer steps coincide with faster completion, which is consistent with a procedural cause.
The two schemes are not comparable, because the median hides the range of waiting times.

options.text: Cutting five steps coincided with a 28-day fall, so the revised scheme is clearly better than the old one.
options.misconception: assumes one observed difference settles which scheme is best

questions.learningObjective: Name the practice that shows appointments are made on merit
questions.stem: Revision note REV-212 asks the group to name the practice that most clearly indicates appointments are made on merit.

options.text: The successful candidate is told they were chosen because of their party loyalty.
options.misconception: treats a stated loyalty as evidence of merit

options.text: The post is advertised only to people already known to the hiring panel.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the argument that surviving an election proves durability
questions.stem: Revision note REV-228 asks the group to evaluate the argument that a policy becomes durable once it has survived a change of government.

answer.exemplar: A policy that survives one change of government has demonstrated that its support is not confined to the officials who introduced it, which is real evidence of durability, but it is evidence about one test rather than a guarantee about the next. Durability of this kind is usually built gradually: a policy gains its own constituency of administrators and beneficiaries, it becomes entangled with funding and statutory duties that make repeal costly, and it acquires sunk costs that make a new government prefer to administer it rather than dismantle it. The defensible position is therefore that surviving a change of government is a milestone in the building of support rather than the completion of it, and that the analyst should look for these reinforcing mechanisms rather than treating a single electoral test as conclusive.

questions.explanation: Surviving one change of government is evidence of self-reinforcing support, not proof of permanence. The tempting claim treats a single test as conclusive and asserts a re-legislative rule.
questions.hint: Ask what makes repeal costly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the argument that bureaucracy is needed for fairness
questions.stem: Revision note REV-284 asks the group to evaluate the argument that bureaucratic organisation is necessary for fair treatment.

answer.exemplar: The argument is substantially right, and the team should be able to say why without overstating it. A large organisation serving many people cannot rely on individual judgement about individual cases, because that would produce different answers for people in identical situations, and the persons best placed to press for an exception are usually the ones with the resources to make the case. Written rules, equal criteria and a recorded trail of decisions are what make similar cases receive similar treatment, and the discipline of following them is what protects the less powerful from being refused at the counter. The qualification the group should add is that equal treatment through the procedure is not by itself fair treatment of the underlying need, since a rule applied evenly to unequal cases can produce unequal outcomes, and the obligation to check that the rule is reasonable is what stops equal application becoming its own kind of injustice.

questions.explanation: Equal application of written rules protects people in similar situations from unequal treatment, which is the core of the argument. The tempting objection ignores case-by-case discretion.
questions.hint: Ask what replaces individual favour.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that the gap is a motivation problem
questions.stem: Revision note REV-320 asks the group to evaluate the argument that the implementation gap is mainly a problem of administrative motivation.

answer.exemplar: The argument identifies one real contributor among several and treats it as the whole account, and the team should be able to say which parts of the gap it does and does not explain. Where staff are indifferent to the policy, have no resources to apply it, or have been given goals that pull in different directions, delivery will be poor whatever their attitude; attention and commitment matter, but only once capacity and clarity are in place. The gap also has a structural side, because the people who decided a policy are not the people who must deliver it, and the delivery organisations work to their own routines, targets and professional norms, which may not match the intention of the decision. The defensible conclusion is that motivation explains part of the variation in delivery between comparable policies, but that a fuller account must include capacity, procedural design and the distance between deciding and delivering, since treating the gap as a motivation problem leaves the structural causes untouched.

questions.explanation: Motivation is one contributor, but capacity, procedure and the gap between deciding and delivering explain much of it. The tempting reduction to attitude leaves structural causes untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what else delivery depends on.

questions.stem: Revision note REV-328 asks the group to explain why red tape is often hardest for the people with the least capacity to comply.

options.text: Because small firms cannot afford the staff time that compliance requires.
options.misconception: explains the burden by cost to the applicant

options.text: Because small firms are less familiar with the rules that larger ones employ.
options.misconception: assumes familiarity is the only problem

options.text: Because the same fixed procedural burden takes a larger share of a small capacity.
Because the rules were written with larger organisations in mind and ignore them.
options.misconception: claims the rules deliberately exclude small firms

questions.explanation: A fixed procedural burden falls hardest on the least capacity, because compliance has a cost floor that does not shrink with scale. The distractors explain it by cost, familiarity and exclusion.
questions.hint: Ask how the burden scales with size.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a recruitment process from its log

stimulus.body: The log records that the panel for a senior post interviewed four candidates against published criteria, scored each interview, and recorded 41, 38, 29 and 22 points. The log also records that the successful candidate was the only one invited to meet the minister who had nominated them, and the minister described the appointment afterwards as an appointment of someone he trusted.

questions.stem: Revision note REV-332 asks the group to assess the process described in the log.

options.text: The process was sound, because a published scoring process was followed for all four candidates.
options.misconception: treats a scored process as the whole of the decision

options.text: The process mixed a scored process with an unrecorded political preference.
The process was unsound, because the minister's description proves the outcome was fixed in advance.
options.misconception: treats a public statement as proof of a fixed outcome

options.text: The process was unsound, because the interview scores were too close together to decide it.
options.misconception: invents a requirement for a clear score gap

questions.explanation: A scored panel followed by separate access for the nominee mixes a merit process with a political one. The distractors treat the scoring as the whole decision and read a public statement as proof.
questions.hint: Ask what the log records besides the scores.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the waiting time removed by a process review
questions.stem: Revision note REV-336 asks the group to work out how many days of waiting are removed in total if 180 requests each lose 3 days from a review of the process.
questions.explanation: One hundred and eighty requests saving three days each removes 540 days of waiting in total. The tempting error averages the saving instead of totalling it, or multiplies in the wrong order.
questions.hint: Multiply requests by days saved.
